---
title: "Objects talking to each other: callbacks and Maps"
---

A `ToolSelection` object owns the tool buttons and knows which tool the user
picked. A `StatusLine` object writes that tool onto the page. The two have to
agree, and how you connect them decides whether the page does a few clicks of
work or sixty checks a second.

## A status line that keeps asking {#sec-callbacks-maps-experiment}

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Tool selection</h1>
   <button id="circleTool" type="button">Circle</button>
   <button id="rectTool" type="button">Rectangle</button>
   <p id="statusLine"></p>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Create `src/tool-selection.ts`:

   ```ts
   export type ToolType = 'circle' | 'rect';

   export class ToolSelection {
     private currentToolValue: ToolType = 'circle';

     constructor() {
       const circleButton = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#circleTool');
       const rectButton = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#rectTool');
       if (!circleButton || !rectButton) {
         throw new Error('A tool button is missing');
       }

       circleButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
         this.currentToolValue = 'circle';
       });
       rectButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
         this.currentToolValue = 'rect';
       });
     }

     get currentTool(): ToolType {
       return this.currentToolValue;
     }
   }
   ```

4. Create `src/status-line.ts`:

   ```ts
   import type { ToolType } from './tool-selection';

   export class StatusLine {
     private paragraph: HTMLParagraphElement;
     private updates = 0;

     constructor() {
       const paragraph = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#statusLine');
       if (!paragraph) {
         throw new Error('No element with the id statusLine');
       }
       this.paragraph = paragraph;
     }

     show(tool: ToolType): void {
       this.updates += 1;
       this.paragraph.textContent = `Tool: ${tool} (updated ${this.updates} times)`;
     }
   }
   ```

   `ToolType` is a type, not a class, so the import gets the word `type` in
   front of the braces. That says out loud that nothing from this line
   survives into the finished JavaScript. Leave the `type` out and `npm run
   check` asks you for it.

5. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   import { StatusLine } from './status-line';
   import { ToolSelection } from './tool-selection';

   const toolSelection = new ToolSelection();
   const statusLine = new StatusLine();

   const tick = () => {
     statusLine.show(toolSelection.currentTool);
     requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   };
   requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   ```

6. Run `npm start` and watch the paragraph.

The tool name is right, and it changes the instant you click. The counter is
the problem. It climbs by roughly 60 a second, so it is in the hundreds before
your first click, and every one of those updates asked a question whose answer
had not changed. Asking over and over like this is called polling, and it is
the crude way to connect two objects.

Now let the `ToolSelection` speak instead. In `src/tool-selection.ts`, add
this line above the class:

```ts
export type ToolChangeCallback = (tool: ToolType) => void;
```

Add the field next to `currentToolValue` and the two methods to the class.
Both click listeners now call `this.selectTool('circle')` and
`this.selectTool('rect')` instead of assigning the field directly:

```ts
private toolChangeCallback: ToolChangeCallback | undefined = undefined;

onToolChange(callback: ToolChangeCallback): void {
  this.toolChangeCallback = callback;
}

private selectTool(tool: ToolType): void {
  this.currentToolValue = tool;
  if (this.toolChangeCallback) {
    this.toolChangeCallback(tool);
  }
}
```

Then throw the animation loop out of `src/index.ts` and hand a function over
instead:

```ts
toolSelection.onToolChange((tool) => {
  statusLine.show(tool);
});
```

Reload. The paragraph starts empty, because nothing has happened yet. Click
Rectangle and it reads `Tool: rect (updated 1 times)`. Click again and the
counter goes to 2. Two updates for two clicks, where the loop did hundreds for
none.

## A function you hand over {#sec-callbacks-maps-callback}

The function you passed to `onToolChange` is a **callback**: you give another
object a function, that object keeps it, and it calls the function back when
it has something to say. You have been handing out callbacks since Part 2,
because the arrow function inside `addEventListener('click', ...)` is exactly
that. What is new here is that you write the receiving side yourself.

The type says the whole story in one line:

```ts
export type ToolChangeCallback = (tool: ToolType) => void;
```

Read it out loud as "a function that takes a `ToolType` and gives nothing
back". Any function of that shape fits, so the caller decides what actually
happens and `ToolSelection` never learns that a status line exists. The button
owner announces, the receiver reacts, and neither one imports the other.

The field is `ToolChangeCallback | undefined` because nobody may have
registered yet, which is why `selectTool` checks before it calls. Registering
twice replaces the first function, so this class serves one listener. That is
enough for every app in this book.

Whoever registers a callback still learns nothing until the first click, which
is why the status line sits empty on a fresh page. Fix that where the
knowledge lives, by calling the new callback once with the current value:

```ts
onToolChange(callback: ToolChangeCallback): void {
  this.toolChangeCallback = callback;
  callback(this.currentToolValue);
}
```

## Properties that may be missing {#sec-callbacks-maps-optional}

Three tool buttons need a label each, and some deserve a tooltip that explains
what the tool does. A question mark after a property name says "this one may
be absent":

```ts
type ToolInfo = {
  kind: ToolType;
  label: string;
  hint?: string;
};

const toolInfos: ToolInfo[] = [
  { kind: 'pointer', label: 'Pointer', hint: 'Click a shape to select it' },
  { kind: 'circle', label: 'Circle' },
];
```

Both entries compile. Reading `info.hint` gives you `string | undefined`, so
TypeScript makes you check before you use it, the same way it does after a
`querySelector`:

```ts
if (info.hint) {
  button.title = info.hint;
}
```

Skip the check and the compiler says `Type 'string | undefined' is not
assignable to type 'string'`.

::: {.callout-note}
## A missing property is not a property set to undefined

The starter's `tsconfig.json` switches on `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, so
writing `{ kind: 'circle', label: 'Circle', hint: undefined }` is refused: with
a `?` the property is either there or it is not, and there is no third state.
When a **field** of a class has to be emptied again later, drop the `?` and
declare it as `private drawing: DrawingState | undefined = undefined;`. Then
assigning `undefined` back to it is fine.
:::

## A Map is a lookup table {#sec-callbacks-maps-map}

When a third tool button arrives, `ToolSelection` has to un-highlight the
other two whenever one is picked, and one field per button gets old fast. A
`Map` holds pairs, so one field carries all three:

```ts
private buttons: Map<ToolType, HTMLButtonElement> = new Map();
```

The two types in the brackets say what the keys are and what the values are,
just like `querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>` says what comes back. Part 6
shows how to write brackets like these on your own classes; until then, read
them and use them.

You put a pair in with `set`, ask for one with `get`, ask whether a key exists
with `has`, throw a pair out with `delete`, and count with `size`:

```ts
this.buttons.set(info.kind, button);

const activeButton = this.buttons.get(tool);
if (activeButton) {
  activeButton.classList.add('active');
}
```

That `if` is not optional. `get` gives back `HTMLButtonElement | undefined`,
because no map can promise that a key is in it. Looping goes over the values,
the keys, or both, and a `Map` keeps the order you inserted the pairs in:

```ts
for (const button of this.buttons.values()) {
  button.classList.remove('active');
}
```

The [MDN page about
Map](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map)
lists far more than you need today, so look up what a task asks for.

## A Set holds each value once {#sec-callbacks-maps-set}

Give the `ToolSelection` of your experiment one more field:

```ts
private usedTools: Set<ToolType> = new Set();
```

Then put two more lines at the top of `selectTool`, reload, and click around
with the console open:

```ts
this.usedTools.add(tool);
console.log(`${this.usedTools.size} of 2 tools tried`);
```

Ten clicks on Circle, and the size stays at 1. A `Set` is a bag of values
where each value fits in only once, so `add` on something already in there
changes nothing. It answers `has`, drops a value with `delete`, counts with
`size`, and iterates with `for...of` in insertion order.

The method worth the switch is `delete`. Pulling one shape out of an array
means finding its index first, while a `Set` takes the shape itself. Paint
keeps its shapes in a `Set` for that reason, and its buttons in a `Map`
because a button does have a name you look it up by.

## enum or union literal type {#sec-callbacks-maps-enum}

TypeScript has a second way to write a small fixed list of choices:

```ts
enum ToolType {
  CIRCLE,
  RECT,
  POINTER,
}
```

`ToolType.CIRCLE` then behaves like a value you can pass around, and
`console.log(ToolType.CIRCLE)` prints `0`, because the members are numbered
from zero unless you spell out something else. That number is what lands in
your log and in anything you save, so debugging means translating `2` back
into `POINTER` in your head.

This course uses union literal types instead:

```ts
type ToolType = 'pointer' | 'circle' | 'rect';
```

The value is the string, so `console.log(tool)` prints `pointer`, a class name
or an attribute takes it unchanged, and the compiler still refuses `'pointr'`.
An `enum` also leaves a real object behind in the compiled JavaScript, while a
union literal type vanishes completely. Read `enum` when you meet it in other
people's code, and write union literal types in yours.

::: {.research title="Pointers, capture, and dashes"}
Paint draws while you drag, keeps drawing when the mouse wanders off the
canvas, and shows the shape you are dragging with a dashed outline. The
chapter covers none of the three.

1. The browser fires `mousedown` and it fires `pointerdown`. What does the
   pointer family handle that the mouse family does not, and which three
   pointer events does one drag need from press to release?
2. `element.setPointerCapture(...)` wants one number. Where do you get that
   number, and what changes about the events after the call?
3. In CSS, `stroke-dasharray` turns a solid outline into a dashed one. What do
   the two numbers in a value such as `6 4` mean?

Question 1 is exam material. Every draw-by-dragging task starts with picking
the right event family, and the exam has no internet and no AI.
:::

## Exercise: Paint {#sec-callbacks-maps-exercise}

A toolbar picks a tool, dragging on the canvas draws a circle or a rectangle,
the pointer tool selects a shape, and a button deletes it. This is the biggest
app of the part, so it comes in three rounds that each end with something you
can run.

{{< exercise paint >}}

### Round 1: the toolbar and its callback {#sec-callbacks-maps-round1}

1. Open `index.html` and read it. The `<div id="toolButtons">` is empty
   because your code fills it, the **Delete selected** button starts out
   `disabled`, the `<svg id="canvas">` has a `viewBox` of `0 0 600 400`, and a
   `<p id="statusLine">` sits under everything.
2. Create `src/tool-selection.ts`. Export
   `type ToolType = 'pointer' | 'circle' | 'rect';` and the
   `ToolChangeCallback` type from this chapter.
3. In the same file, add the `ToolInfo` type with `kind`, `label`, and an
   optional `hint`, and a `const toolInfos: ToolInfo[]` holding the three
   tools. Give Pointer and Rectangle a hint and leave Circle without one.
4. Write and export `class ToolSelection` with three fields: a
   `Map<ToolType, HTMLButtonElement>`, the current tool starting at
   `'pointer'`, and the callback field.
5. The constructor takes a `container: HTMLElement`. Loop over `toolInfos`
   and for each one create a `button`, set its `type` to `'button'` and its
   `textContent` to the label, set `button.title` only when the hint is there,
   add a click listener that calls `this.selectTool(info.kind)`, put the
   button into the map under `info.kind`, and append it to the container. End
   the constructor with `this.selectTool('pointer')`.
6. Write the private method `selectTool(tool: ToolType)`. It stores the tool,
   removes the class `active` from every button in the map, adds `active` to
   the button the map has for this tool, and calls the callback if one is
   registered.
7. Write `onToolChange(callback: ToolChangeCallback)`. It stores the callback
   and calls it once with the current tool.
8. Create `src/index.ts`. Import `./styles.css`, look up `#toolButtons` with
   `querySelector<HTMLDivElement>` and throw when it is missing, then build a
   `ToolSelection` around it and register a callback that logs the tool with
   `console.log`.
9. Run `npm start`. Expected result: three buttons, Pointer highlighted, and
   the console shows the tool name once on load and once per click. Hover a
   button and the hint appears; hover Circle and nothing appears.

### Round 2: drawing circles and rectangles {#sec-callbacks-maps-round2}

1. Create `src/point.ts` with
   `export type Point = { x: number; y: number; };`. Every other file imports
   it with `import type { Point } from './point';`, the type-only import from
   the polymorphism chapter, because `Point` is a type and not a class.
2. Create `src/shape.ts`. Put `const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';`
   at the top and export an `abstract class Shape` with a
   `protected element: SVGElement`. Its constructor takes
   `(canvas: SVGSVGElement, tagName: string)`, creates the element with
   `createElementNS`, and appends it to the canvas.
3. Give `Shape` three abstract members: `resize(start: Point, end: Point)`,
   `containsPoint(point: Point): boolean`, and a getter
   `isTooSmall: boolean`.
4. Give `Shape` four normal members: a setter `preview` that adds or removes
   the class `preview`, `select()` and `deselect()` that add and remove the
   class `selected`, and `remove()` that calls `remove()` on the element.
5. Create `src/circle.ts` with `class Circle extends Shape`, whose
   constructor passes `'circle'` to `super`. It stores a center and a radius.
   `resize` puts the center at `start`, takes the distance from `start` to
   `end` as the radius, and writes `cx`, `cy`, and `r` with `setAttribute`.
   `containsPoint` compares the distance to the radius, and `isTooSmall` is
   true below radius 3.
6. Create `src/rect.ts` the same way with `'rect'`. `resize` uses the smaller
   `x` and the smaller `y` as the corner and the absolute differences as
   `width` and `height`, `containsPoint` checks both ranges, and `isTooSmall`
   is true when either side is under 3.
7. Create `src/shape-manager.ts` and export `class ShapeManager`. It needs
   four fields: the canvas, `shapes: Set<Shape>`, the current tool starting at
   `'pointer'`, and `drawing: DrawingState | undefined` with this type in the
   same file:

    ```ts
    type DrawingState = {
      shape: Shape;
      start: Point;
    };
    ```

    Add a public `setTool(tool: ToolType)` that stores the tool.
8. In the constructor, listen on the canvas for the three pointer events from
   the research box, each handler a private method.
9. Write a private `positionOf(event: PointerEvent): Point` that turns
   `event.clientX` and `event.clientY` into canvas coordinates with the
   `getBoundingClientRect` subtraction you used for SVG drawings. The `<svg>`
   is 600 pixels wide and 600 viewBox units wide, so the numbers match one to
   one.
10. On press, work out the position with `positionOf` first, then leave at
    once while the tool is `'pointer'`. Otherwise capture the pointer with the
    method from the research box, build a `Circle` or a `Rect`, set its
    `preview` to `true`, call `resize(point, point)`, and store the drawing
    state.
11. On move: leave when nothing is being drawn, otherwise call `resize` with
    the stored start point and the current position.
12. On release: leave when nothing is being drawn. Otherwise clear the drawing
    state, take the shape off the canvas again when it `isTooSmall`, and
    otherwise set `preview` to `false` and add it to the set.
13. Add a rule for `#canvas .preview` to `src/styles.css` that gives the
    outline the dashed pattern from the research box, plus a
    `fill-opacity: 0.3;` so you can see through the shape while you drag.
14. In `src/index.ts`, look up `#canvas` as an `SVGSVGElement` in the same
    `if` as the toolbar, build a `ShapeManager` around it, and change the tool
    callback so it calls `shapeManager.setTool(tool)`.
15. Run the app. Expected result: with Circle picked, dragging draws a dashed
    circle that grows with the mouse and turns solid blue when you let go.
    Rectangle does the same in red. Drag past the edge of the canvas and the
    shape keeps following the mouse. A single click with no drag leaves
    nothing behind. Pointer draws nothing yet.

### Round 3: selecting and deleting {#sec-callbacks-maps-round3}

1. In `src/shape-manager.ts`, add a field `selected: Shape | undefined`, a
   second callback type, and a field that holds one of them:

   ```ts
   export type ShapesChangedCallback = (shapeCount: number, hasSelection: boolean) => void;
   ```
2. Add `onShapesChanged(callback: ShapesChangedCallback)`. Like
   `onToolChange`, it stores the callback and calls it once, with
   `this.shapes.size` and whether something is selected.
3. Add a private `reportChange()` that calls the stored callback with those
   same two values when one is registered, and call it at the end of the
   release handler.
4. Add a private `selectAt(point: Point)`. It deselects every shape in the
   set and clears `selected`, then walks the set and remembers the last shape
   whose `containsPoint(point)` is true. Select that shape when there is one,
   and call `reportChange()` either way. The last match wins because a `Set`
   keeps insertion order, so the shape drawn last sits on top.
5. In the press handler, replace the early return for the pointer tool with a
   call to `selectAt(point)`.
6. Add a public `deleteSelected()`. It does nothing when nothing is selected.
   Otherwise it calls `remove()` on the shape, deletes it from the set, clears
   the selection, and calls `reportChange()`.
7. In `src/index.ts`, add `#deleteButton` and `#statusLine` to the lookup and
   to the `if`. Register a callback on the shape manager that sets
   `deleteButton.disabled` from `hasSelection` and writes
   `` `${shapeCount} shapes on the canvas` `` into the status line. Give the
   button a click listener that calls `shapeManager.deleteSelected()`.
8. Run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, then run the app. Expected
   result: the page starts with `0 shapes on the canvas` and a grayed-out
   Delete button, and drawing raises the count. With Pointer picked, clicking
   a shape gives it a yellow outline and enables Delete, while clicking empty
   space clears the selection and disables Delete again. Delete takes the
   shape away and the count drops.
9. Bonus: keep a `Set<ToolType>` of the tools that were used and show
   `2 of 3 tools tried` in the status line next to the shape count.
